title: The ultimate horse - Works in Progress Magazine
excerpt: Selective breeding has pushed horses to the limits of biology. But at what cost?
content_html:
In June 1973, chestnut colt Secretariat ran the Belmont Stakes so fast that no horse has matched him since. In less than two and a half minutes, Secretariat flew along the track, finally pulling away to win by 31 lengths, nearly three quarters of a football field. The other horses were so far behind they weren’t even in the television frame. Fifty years later, billions of dollars have been poured into breeding and training, yet Secretariat’s record still stands.

This is the paradox of the thoroughbred: breeders have spent centuries trying to create a faster horse, but in doing so, they may have bred away the very genetic diversity that would allow the horse to keep improving, or even to remain robust.

The paradox is not confined to the racetrack. The horse began as a terrier-sized, multi-toed forest dweller and, over 55 million years of evolution and a few thousand years of human intervention, became everything from the compact Icelandic pony to the streamlined racehorse. For most of that history, natural selection shaped horses slowly. Only recently has human ambition taken over, breeding animals for speed, endurance, and docility. The result is extraordinary diversity in form and performance, but also a dramatic narrowing of genetic diversity.

The first horses

The story begins 55 million years ago, deep in the warm, humid forests that covered what is now North America. You’d be hard pressed to recognize the earliest equid. Known as Hyracotherium, it stood only 14 inches tall, closer to a terrier than a modern horse. With four toes on the front feet and three on the back, it was ideally suited to moving gingerly over soft, marshy ground and nibbling fruits and leaves.

When global temperatures rose, between 18 and 15 million years ago, the equid family diversified into more than twenty genera (the subdivision above species living in woodlands and savannas). Most of these lineages have long since died out: today, only the genus Equus survives, which includes horses, zebras, asses, and donkeys.

As grasslands spread, over millions of years, equids developed into the horses we see today. Few evolutionary stories are as well documented. In the nineteenth century, when paleontologist OC Marsh unearthed a rich collection of fossil horses in the American West, their significance was immediately recognized. Here, laid out almost step by step, was evolution in action: horses transitioning from small, many-toed forest-dwellers into large, single-toed animals that grazed on grass rather than eating fruit and leaves.

That single toe, of which the hoof is the toenail, is the evolutionary innovation key to horses’ success. Life on the plains favored animals able to run efficiently over long distances. Rigid, lightweight hooves help with this: they minimize sideways wobble while storing and releasing energy like a spring, much like the shoes a human sprinter might wear, or even the prosthetic running blades sometimes used by amputees.

Over millions of years, the number of toes fell gradually from several to just one. Between 43 and 33 million years ago, Mesohippus still sported three toes of roughly equal size, with each touching the ground. By the time of Hipparion, about 23 million years ago, the middle toe carried most of the animal’s weight: the outer two toes had shrunk into vestiges, and the middle toe had become dominant. Finally, Pliohippus took a pivotal step toward the modern form, with a single weight-bearing toe ending in a solid hoof. This evolutionary streamlining produced the feet of today’s horses: a single, sturdy keratin hoof perfectly suited for galloping over open ground.

The route to the modern horse involved several detours. Hyracotherium, the progenitor of the horse family, appears in the fossil record in North America from around 55 million years ago, disappearing again 8 million years later. Around 12 million years ago, Hipparion, which, though three-toed, otherwise resembled modern horses, colonized Eurasia. Hippidion, which had short limbs and distinctively shaped facial bones, roamed the plains and mountains of South America from around 3 million years ago. Then, around 2 million years ago, the most recent common ancestor of present-day asses and zebras crossed the Bering land bridge formerly joining Alaska and northeastern Siberia.

Within the next half a million years, their descendants rapidly expanded across Eurasia and entered Africa at least two separate times. The descendants of the first migration diversified into various zebras, while the second led to modern donkeys and African wild asses.

Although the Americas were home to the earliest proto-horses, horses (including Hippidion and others) later became extinct in the Western Hemisphere around 10,000 years ago, alongside other megafauna like giant sloths, human-sized beavers, and armadillos as big as cars. All horses in the Americas today, including the free-roaming mustangs of the American West, come from European horses introduced after the Spanish conquest – descendants of the branches of the horse family that crossed into Eurasia and avoided extinction.

The first horse tamers

Exactly when, where, and how horses were domesticated remained a mystery until recently, because fossils of wild and early domestic horses look very similar. For decades, archaeologists pointed to the Botai people of northern Kazakhstan, who lived around 5,500 years ago, as the original domesticators. Excavations revealed corrals, possible evidence of harnesses, and even pottery with residues of horse milk, a clear sign that the Botai people were not merely hunting and eating wild horses but had integrated them into many aspects of their lives.

While the Botai horses seemed like the obvious ancestors of modern horses, DNA told a different story: when scientists sequenced the genomes of twenty horses from the Botai site, they were not genetically similar to modern domestic breeds. Instead, Botai horses grouped closely with the Przewalski’s horse (pronounced shuh-VAHL-ski), a species discovered roaming the Mongolian steppe in the late 1870s and long considered the only truly wild horse.

This means that, contrary to the long-held belief that Przewalski’s horses were the last surviving truly wild horses, they are instead the feral relatives of the earliest known domestic horses found at Botai. While the Botai likely did domesticate horses first, their culture died out and their horses returned to the wild.

From steppe to stable

The horses we know and love came from a different source. They emerged more than a thousand years later, about 4,200 years ago, in the Pontic-Caspian steppes of what is now southern Russia, the same region that gave rise to famous horse-riding warriors like the Cossacks, the Golden Horde, and the Huns.

Scientists have worked this out through genetic analysis of ancient horse remains, combined with carbon dating to establish their precise age. A foal inherits half of its DNA from each of its parents. This is passed on with almost incredible accuracy, with around 2.7 billion base pairs (the data units of DNA) being copied correctly, but even so a few dozen errors creep in each time. A scientist can take the DNA of an ancient ancestor from a fossil, compare it with the DNA of a modern descendant, and then estimate how many generations have passed by counting the number of mutations that have accumulated.

In 2021, scientists did just this, sequencing genomes from 273 sets of bones ranging from 50,000 to 200 years old. By looking at the mutation rate and carbon dating the bones to confirm their exact age, they could calculate how quickly generations passed. About 4,200 years ago, the generational clock began to tick twice as fast, halving relative to wild horses, suggesting deliberate breeding.

Although bones can’t tell us how ancient horses behaved, their genomes give us clues. The researchers found that certain genetic variants became unusually common in these steppe horses. Such a pattern signals strong selective pressure: something in the environment consistently favored animals carrying particular versions of genes. 

One region under heavy selection lies near a gene called ZFPM1, thought to play a role in the development of brain cells involved in mood, fear, and aggression. This suggests that early breeders might have been either deliberately or indirectly choosing animals that were more docile, allowing training, handling, and eventually riding. A second region under strong selection sits just upstream of GSDMC, a gene linked in humans to spinal problems such as chronic back pain and narrowing of the spinal canal. The signal of selection at this locus in horses suggests that breeders may have favored genetic variants associated with stronger, more resilient backs. As horseback riding spread, horses that could bear weight without developing spinal pathologies would have been more desirable.

These steppe horses, known to geneticists as DOM2 (that is, domesticated lineage two), spread like wildfire. By 2200 to 2000 BC, the DOM2 genetic profile spread beyond its region of origin to Anatolia, the lower Danube region, and Bohemia.

Archaeological evidence suggests that as DOM2 expanded, the populations of other wild horses gradually dwindled. By around 1500–1000 BC, almost all had been either absorbed or replaced. The tarpan horse, which roamed Eastern Europe, became extinct in 1909. By 1969, Przewalski’s horse was declared extinct in the wild. All living Przewalski’s horses stem from just 15 individuals captured around the year 1900. Only in 1992 did the descendants, numbering about 2,000, begin to be reintroduced on the Eurasian steppes. 

The many so-called wild horse populations found around the world, including mustangs, Sable Island ponies, and Australian brumbies, all descend from modern domestic horses that became feral again within the past few centuries.

Horses for courses

Over time, humans developed distinct horse breeds with a wide range of phenotypes, from the tiny Argentinian Falabella, barely reaching a meter tall at the shoulder, to the towering French Percheron, capable of hauling tons; from horses with the standard gaits (walk, trot, canter, and gallop) to horses able to perform alternative gaits, like ambling, with no bounce, making them more comfortable to ride. The Icelandic horse's tölt is so smooth that a rider can carry a full glass of beer without spilling a drop.

This diversity is the product of millennia of human intervention, selection, and preference, which left distinct traces in the horse’s genome. Compared with many other species, horses have a lot of diversity in the mitochondrial genome, inherited from the mother, but extremely limited variation within the Y chromosome, passed down from father to son. This contrast suggests a pattern in domestication: many local mares (female horses) were bred with a fairly narrow pool of stallions (males), concentrating paternal lineages while preserving variety in the maternal line.

Ancient DNA has given us a window beyond fossils, allowing us to track how phenotypes changed in ways that don’t show up in the fossil record. After humans, horses are one of the species ancient genomics has studied the most. In fact, the very first successful recovery and analysis of ancient DNA was from 150-year-old tissue from the extinct quagga, a close relative of the zebra, in 1984 – a year before the same was achieved with ancient human DNA. One of the oldest genomes ever successfully recovered and decoded comes from a horse bone preserved in the Yukon permafrost for over half a million years.

Coat color offers another window into early horse breeding. In living horses, the genes behind colors and patterns, like leopard spotting, tobiano patches (like the coloring of a cow), and cream dilutions (that lighten the color of a horse’s coat), are well understood. Genetic variants for dun (gray-gold, or tan), black, and leopard spotting appear in wild horses from the Upper Paleolithic, long before domestication began.

In the early Bronze Age, leopard-spotted horses were abundant at Kirklareli-Kanlıgeçit in present-day Turkey. But leopard spotting comes at a cost: horses with two copies of the gene coding for it have night blindness (the inability to see in low light). Its prevalence in certain ancient populations suggests breeders made deliberate choices, where aesthetic or symbolic value outweighed the trait’s practical drawbacks, to favor certain traits unlikely to persist in the wild. Tastes shifted with time: leopard-spotted horses lost their appeal after the early Bronze Age but gained favor in some regions during the Iron Age. And while spotted coats were popular in antiquity, solid chestnut horses prevailed in medieval Western Europe.

In the Middle Ages, horses were inseparable from power and status. Chivalry itself shares an etymological root with the Old French chevalier, literally ‘horseman’. Breeding and maintaining horses became a major industry of nobility and royalty. But they didn’t think in terms of fixed breeds the way we do today. Medieval writers grouped horses by function: the destrier trained for combat, the courser valued for speed, and the palfrey prized for a comfortable ride. Archaeological evidence backs this up. A large study of horse remains from thirteenth- and fourteenth-century London shows a range of sizes and builds, not the uniformity that we would expect from tightly restricted breeding.

Contrary to the modern idea of the medieval warhorse as a massive, towering beast, measurements from excavated horse bones across England show that most stood around 13 to 14.2 hands high, roughly the size of a sturdy modern pony. Even horses associated with elite or military contexts rarely approached the heights of today’s heavy draught breeds. What medieval riders valued instead were animals that were compact (meaning cheap to feed), strong, and agile enough to handle long distances, uneven terrain, and the demands of warfare.

The need for speed

By the seventeenth century, horses had been serving human purposes for thousands of years, plowing fields, carrying soldiers, and pulling carts. But in early-modern England, one goal came to dominate: speed. In the 1660s, King Charles II, a fervent horse racing fan, set up a horse breeding and racing center at Newmarket, near London. While horse racing had been popular in previous centuries, Charles II and other racing enthusiasts were the first to methodically breed horses at scale to improve their race performance.

Breeders discovered that horses from Arabia, Central Asia, and North Africa were often faster: they were lighter, had a greater drive to run, and were better able to dissipate heat, allowing them to sustain high speeds without overheating. From three exceptional horses imported to England, Byerley Turk (imported in the 1680s), Darley Arabian (1704), and Godolphin Arabian (1729), breeders created the ‘thoroughbred’, a new type of horse designed for speed. Today, 95 percent of all living thoroughbreds are thought to descend from just one of these stallions, Darley Arabian, through his phenomenally successful great-great-grandson, Eclipse.

Horse breeding used to be guesswork: breeders paired fast stallions with fast mares and hoped for the best. But in 1791, the General Stud Book started recording every thoroughbred’s ancestry, turning pedigree into data. Breeders could now track bloodlines, deliberately plan matings, and see which combinations actually worked. Thoroughbreds today are defined as horses whose ancestry can be traced entirely to horses listed in the General Stud Book.

Harder, better, faster, stronger

Racing and breeding evolved side by side. Races in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries involved multiple heats over distances of two to four miles, favoring horses with stamina. Horses didn’t race until they were five or six years old. But by the late eighteenth century, new races like the Derby and the St Leger reset the terms of competition. Horses now raced at three years old, over shorter distances of one to two miles. 

This new format meant an increased premium on speed and precocity, and it has persisted, particularly in the United States and Australia. In Britain and Ireland, the tradition of long-distance races held on in parallel, leading to distinct types: horses that specialize in explosive speed at a young age, classic middle-distance horses, and horses bred for the stamina needed to excel in longer races.

After the creation of the thoroughbred and the Stud Book, Anglo-American breeders hit what appears to be an upper limit for speed surprisingly quickly. From the middle of the nineteenth century, when timing and record keeping became good enough to make reliable comparisons, race times improved steadily for about half a century. But although there was consistent improvement, it was small: times only fell by 1 to 2 percent, or 2 to 4 seconds over a 1.5-mile race. Race times for prominent races have not significantly fallen since around 1910. Secretariat’s 1973 Belmont time eclipsed the previous record by a stunning 2.6 seconds. However, the best time since then (Easy Goer in 1989 at 2 minutes 26 seconds) was a full 2 seconds slower than Secretariat’s.

Outside the elite, there has been continued improvement: one study found that between 1997 and 2012, accounting for differences such as ground softness and the number of runners, the average British thoroughbred increased its speed by 0.011 yards per second per year. So while we have likely reached the ceiling for how fast an exceptional horse can run, the median horse is beginning to close in on that limit, too.

The genes for speed

Until 2007, the Stud Book was the cutting edge of horse breeding technology. That changed when scientists sequenced a horse genome for the first time, that of a thoroughbred mare named Twilight. This allowed researchers to study the genetic basis of variation between individual horses far more systematically.

Another step forward in understanding thoroughbred genetics came with a paper published in 2010 that investigated the gene in horses that codes for myostatin, a protein that regulates muscle development. Mice, cattle, dogs, and even humans with mutations in this gene grow outlandishly large muscles because the gene normally acts as a brake on muscle development; with that brake damaged, muscles continue to grow unchecked.

The gene coding for myostatin in horses has around 1,100 base pairs. Looking at the exact sequence of this gene, called MSTN, in 148 thoroughbreds revealed that horses could have three different versions of the gene, differing by just one of those base pairs (either a letter ‘C’ or a ‘T’), and that each version was associated with success in different race formats. Horses with two copies of the ‘C’ version tend to be the best sprinters, those with two ‘T’s tend to be high-stamina long-distance runners, and those with one of each tend to fall between the two running profiles.

Later research found that variations in MSTN correspond with different muscle physiology. Horses with the ‘C’ version have a higher proportion of fast-twitch muscle fibers, which enable the explosive bursts of speed required for short-distance sprint racing, while those with the ‘T’ version have a higher proportion of slow-twitch fibers, which allow sustained effort. 

Analyzing the DNA of modern horses and museum specimens then showed that the foundation stallions in the Stud Book all had two copies of the ‘T’ variant, and that the ‘C’ mutation probably entered through local British mares. This new variant entered thoroughbred genomes during the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, as English races like the Derby and St Leger got shorter. But the genetic trend is less pronounced in Britain than the United States, where races are rarely longer than 2,000 meters, and especially than in Australia, which favors 1,000 to 1,400-meter lengths. Commercial tests for this gene are now widely used by breeders and trainers.

The price of success

Horses’ genetic diversity remained large for thousands of years, before collapsing after the introduction of modern breeding. In nature, diversity is maintained by competing selection pressures that balance one trait against another. A wild horse does not just need to be fast. Its bones need to last. It needs to be resistant to disease. Even a domesticated working horse would, before intensive breeding began, face natural constraints on its traits.

In modern thoroughbred breeding, celebrity stallions with the best race records are in high demand. Their owners charge hundreds of thousands of dollars in stud fees, and they can sire perhaps a hundred foals per year. This means that the genes of particular males can quickly sweep to dominance in a population in a way that would be very unusual in nature.

Along with this loss of diversity, modern horses have accumulated harmful mutations as a result of breeding within a small population. In horses as in humans, repeated inbreeding concentrates harmful traits as parents who are related to each other are more likely to share the same mutations, resulting in offspring with two copies of the mutated gene, rather than one mutated copy and one normal copy, which could mask the mutation’s effects.

A genetic analysis of all Australian thoroughbreds, more than 135,000 horses, showed that inbreeding correlates with slower, shorter, and less lucrative careers. Amazingly, ten heavily crossed eighteenth-century ancestors account for over 80 percent of inbreeding in Australian thoroughbreds. Breeders are not blind to these risks. The American Quarter Horse Association, for example, requires breeding stallions to be tested for several genetic diseases.

As genetics has played such a large role in breeding horses, it is small wonder that horse breeders are moving with the frontiers of science. The world’s first cloned horse, called Prometea, was born in 2003. Horse cloning is now big business, despite an American Jockey Club ban, as other equine sports, including show jumping and polo, allow clones.

In 2024, the Argentinian company Kheiron announced the production of the first CRISPR-edited horses: Polo Pureza, an award-winning mare, was the foundation for five gene-edited clones with increased explosive speed. According to reports, the company modified the MSTN gene, so that the animals would develop more muscle fibers and potentially run faster as a result. Even so, the prospects for exceeding current records through gene editing are slim. Today’s racehorses are already tightly optimized for speed, balancing strength against the cost of carrying additional muscle mass. Adding more muscle is relatively low-hanging fruit, and if this were the key to unlocking greater speed, selective breeding would likely already have brought it about.

The thoroughbred paradox

At the Belmont Stakes in 1973, Secretariat ran in a category of his own. His extraordinary performance seems to have been the result of many unlikely factors aligning. After he died, Secretariat’s heart was reportedly measured at almost 10 kilograms – twice as much as normal. This appears to have been a physiological fluke, however, as it isn’t a trait reliably passed down to offspring. Combined with his unusual stamina, exceptionally powerful legs that allowed him to cover 25 feet per stride, favorable race conditions, and a skilled jockey, this produced a race time that has still never been matched half a century later, despite advances in breeding, training, nutrition, and veterinary care.

Secretariat offers a glimpse of the upper limits of biology. But as racehorses have pushed against that limit to become faster and more powerful, their population has become more fragile as the gene pool has narrowed. Our 4,000-year pursuit of the ultimate horse may not have much further to run.

Its prevalence in certain ancient populations suggests breeders made deliberate choices, where aesthetic or symbolic value outweighed the trait’s practical drawbacks, to favor certain traits unlikely to persist in the wild. Tastes shifted with time: leopard-spotted horses lost their appeal after the early Bronze Age but gained favor in some regions during the Iron Age. And while spotted coats were popular in antiquity, solid chestnut horses prevailed in medieval Western Europe.In the Middle Ages, horses were inseparable from power and status. Chivalry itself shares an etymological root with the Old French chevalier, literally ‘horseman’. Breeding and maintaining horses became a major industry of nobility and royalty. But they didn’t think in terms of fixed breeds the way we do today. Medieval writers grouped horses by function: the destrier trained for combat, the courser valued for speed, and the palfrey prized for a comfortable ride. Archaeological evidence backs this up. A large study of horse remains from thirteenth- and fourteenth-century London shows a range of sizes and builds, not the uniformity that we would expect from tightly restricted breeding.Contrary to the modern idea of the medieval warhorse as a massive, towering beast, measurements from excavated horse bones across England show that most stood around 13 to 14.2 hands high, roughly the size of a sturdy modern pony. Even horses associated with elite or military contexts rarely approached the heights of today’s heavy draught breeds. What medieval riders valued instead were animals that were compact (meaning cheap to feed), strong, and agile enough to handle long distances, uneven terrain, and the demands of warfare.The need for speedBy the seventeenth century, horses had been serving human purposes for thousands of years, plowing fields, carrying soldiers, and pulling carts. But in early-modern England, one goal came to dominate: speed. In the 1660s, King Charles II, a fervent horse racing fan, set up a horse breeding and racing center at Newmarket, near London. While horse racing had been popular in previous centuries, Charles II and other racing enthusiasts were the first to methodically breed horses at scale to improve their race performance. A 1671 illustration of a race at Newmarket Heath. Image Yale Center for British Art, Paul Mellon Fund. Breeders discovered that horses from Arabia, Central Asia, and North Africa were often faster: they were lighter, had a greater drive to run, and were better able to dissipate heat, allowing them to sustain high speeds without overheating. From three exceptional horses imported to England, Byerley Turk (imported in the 1680s), Darley Arabian (1704), and Godolphin Arabian (1729), breeders created the ‘thoroughbred’, a new type of horse designed for speed. Today, 95 percent of all living thoroughbreds are thought to descend from just one of these stallions, Darley Arabian, through his phenomenally successful great-great-grandson, Eclipse.Horse breeding used to be guesswork: breeders paired fast stallions with fast mares and hoped for the best. But in 1791, the General Stud Book started recording every thoroughbred’s ancestry, turning pedigree into data. Breeders could now track bloodlines, deliberately plan matings, and see which combinations actually worked. Thoroughbreds today are defined as horses whose ancestry can be traced entirely to horses listed in the General Stud Book.Harder, better, faster, strongerRacing and breeding evolved side by side. Races in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries involved multiple heats over distances of two to four miles, favoring horses with stamina. Horses didn’t race until they were five or six years old. But by the late eighteenth century, new races like the Derby and the St Leger reset the terms of competition. Horses now raced at three years old, over shorter distances of one to two miles. This new format meant an increased premium on speed and precocity, and it has persisted, particularly in the United States and Australia. In Britain and Ireland, the tradition of long-distance races held on in parallel, leading to distinct types: horses that specialize in explosive speed at a young age, classic middle-distance horses, and horses bred for the stamina needed to excel in longer races.After the creation of the thoroughbred and the Stud Book, Anglo-American breeders hit what appears to be an upper limit for speed surprisingly quickly. From the middle of the nineteenth century, when timing and record keeping became good enough to make reliable comparisons, race times improved steadily for about half a century. But although there was consistent improvement, it was small: times only fell by 1 to 2 percent, or 2 to 4 seconds over a 1.5-mile race. Race times for prominent races have not significantly fallen since around 1910. Secretariat’s 1973 Belmont time eclipsed the previous record by a stunning 2.6 seconds. However, the best time since then (Easy Goer in 1989 at 2 minutes 26 seconds) was a full 2 seconds slower than Secretariat’s.Outside the elite, there has been continued improvement: one study found that between 1997 and 2012, accounting for differences such as ground softness and the number of runners, the average British thoroughbred increased its speed by 0.011 yards per second per year. So while we have likely reached the ceiling for how fast an exceptional horse can run, the median horse is beginning to close in on that limit, too. The genes for speedUntil 2007, the Stud Book was the cutting edge of horse breeding technology. That changed when scientists sequenced a horse genome for the first time, that of a thoroughbred mare named Twilight. This allowed researchers to study the genetic basis of variation between individual horses far more systematically.Another step forward in understanding thoroughbred genetics came with a paper published in 2010 that investigated the gene in horses that codes for myostatin, a protein that regulates muscle development. Mice, cattle, dogs, and even humans with mutations in this gene grow outlandishly large muscles because the gene normally acts as a brake on muscle development; with that brake damaged, muscles continue to grow unchecked.The gene coding for myostatin in horses has around 1,100 base pairs. Looking at the exact sequence of this gene, called MSTN, in 148 thoroughbreds revealed that horses could have three different versions of the gene, differing by just one of those base pairs (either a letter ‘C’ or a ‘T’), and that each version was associated with success in different race formats. Horses with two copies of the ‘C’ version tend to be the best sprinters, those with two ‘T’s tend to be high-stamina long-distance runners, and those with one of each tend to fall between the two running profiles.Later research found that variations in MSTN correspond with different muscle physiology. Horses with the ‘C’ version have a higher proportion of fast-twitch muscle fibers, which enable the explosive bursts of speed required for short-distance sprint racing, while those with the ‘T’ version have a higher proportion of slow-twitch fibers, which allow sustained effort. Analyzing the DNA of modern horses and museum specimens then showed that the foundation stallions in the Stud Book all had two copies of the ‘T’ variant, and that the ‘C’ mutation probably entered through local British mares. This new variant entered thoroughbred genomes during the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, as English races like the Derby and St Leger got shorter. But the genetic trend is less pronounced in Britain than the United States, where races are rarely longer than 2,000 meters, and especially than in Australia, which favors 1,000 to 1,400-meter lengths. Commercial tests for this gene are now widely used by breeders and trainers.The price of successHorses’ genetic diversity remained large for thousands of years, before collapsing after the introduction of modern breeding. In nature, diversity is maintained by competing selection pressures that balance one trait against another. A wild horse does not just need to be fast. Its bones need to last. It needs to be resistant to disease. Even a domesticated working horse would, before intensive breeding began, face natural constraints on its traits.In modern thoroughbred breeding, celebrity stallions with the best race records are in high demand. Their owners charge hundreds of thousands of dollars in stud fees, and they can sire perhaps a hundred foals per year. This means that the genes of particular males can quickly sweep to dominance in a population in a way that would be very unusual in nature.Along with this loss of diversity, modern horses have accumulated harmful mutations as a result of breeding within a small population. In horses as in humans, repeated inbreeding concentrates harmful traits as parents who are related to each other are more likely to share the same mutations, resulting in offspring with two copies of the mutated gene, rather than one mutated copy and one normal copy, which could mask the mutation’s effects.A genetic analysis of all Australian thoroughbreds, more than 135,000 horses, showed that inbreeding correlates with slower, shorter, and less lucrative careers. Amazingly, ten heavily crossed eighteenth-century ancestors account for over 80 percent of inbreeding in Australian thoroughbreds. Breeders are not blind to these risks. The American Quarter Horse Association, for example, requires breeding stallions to be tested for several genetic diseases.As genetics has played such a large role in breeding horses, it is small wonder that horse breeders are moving with the frontiers of science. The world’s first cloned horse, called Prometea, was born in 2003. Horse cloning is now big business, despite an American Jockey Club ban, as other equine sports, including show jumping and polo, allow clones.In 2024, the Argentinian company Kheiron announced the production of the first CRISPR-edited horses: Polo Pureza, an award-winning mare, was the foundation for five gene-edited clones with increased explosive speed. According to reports, the company modified the MSTN gene, so that the animals would develop more muscle fibers and potentially run faster as a result. Even so, the prospects for exceeding current records through gene editing are slim. Today’s racehorses are already tightly optimized for speed, balancing strength against the cost of carrying additional muscle mass. Adding more muscle is relatively low-hanging fruit, and if this were the key to unlocking greater speed, selective breeding would likely already have brought it about.The thoroughbred paradoxAt the Belmont Stakes in 1973, Secretariat ran in a category of his own. His extraordinary performance seems to have been the result of many unlikely factors aligning. After he died, Secretariat’s heart was reportedly measured at almost 10 kilograms – twice as much as normal. This appears to have been a physiological fluke, however, as it isn’t a trait reliably passed down to offspring. Combined with his unusual stamina, exceptionally powerful legs that allowed him to cover 25 feet per stride, favorable race conditions, and a skilled jockey, this produced a race time that has still never been matched half a century later, despite advances in breeding, training, nutrition, and veterinary care.Secretariat offers a glimpse of the upper limits of biology. But as racehorses have pushed against that limit to become faster and more powerful, their population has become more fragile as the gene pool has narrowed. Our 4,000-year pursuit of the ultimate horse may not have much further to run.

blocks.html_en: In June 1973, chestnut colt Secretariat ran the Belmont Stakes so fast that no horse has matched him since. In less than two and a half minutes, Secretariat flew along the track, finally pulling away to win by 31 lengths, nearly three quarters of a football field. The other horses were so far behind they weren’t even in the television frame. Fifty years later, billions of dollars have been poured into breeding and training, yet Secretariat’s record still stands.

blocks.html_en: The paradox is not confined to the racetrack. The horse began as a terrier-sized, multi-toed forest dweller and, over 55 million years of evolution and a few thousand years of human intervention, became everything from the compact Icelandic pony to the streamlined racehorse. For most of that history, natural selection shaped horses slowly. Only recently has human ambition taken over, breeding animals for speed, endurance, and docility. The result is extraordinary diversity in form and performance, but also a dramatic narrowing of genetic diversity.

blocks.html_en: The story begins 55 million years ago, deep in the warm, humid forests that covered what is now North America. You’d be hard pressed to recognize the earliest equid. Known as Hyracotherium, it stood only 14 inches tall, closer to a terrier than a modern horse. With four toes on the front feet and three on the back, it was ideally suited to moving gingerly over soft, marshy ground and nibbling fruits and leaves.

Most of these lineages have long since died out: today, only the genus Equus survives, which includes horses, zebras, asses, and donkeys.

blocks.html_en: As grasslands spread, over millions of years, equids developed into the horses we see today. Few evolutionary stories are as well documented. In the nineteenth century, when paleontologist OC Marsh unearthed a rich collection of fossil horses in the American West, their significance was immediately recognized. Here, laid out almost step by step, was evolution in action: horses transitioning from small, many-toed forest-dwellers into large, single-toed animals that grazed on grass rather than eating fruit and leaves.

blocks.html_en: That single toe, of which the hoof is the toenail, is the evolutionary innovation key to horses’ success. Life on the plains favored animals able to run efficiently over long distances. Rigid, lightweight hooves help with this: they minimize sideways wobble while storing and releasing energy like a spring, much like the shoes a human sprinter might wear, or even the prosthetic running blades sometimes used by amputees.

sentences.zh: 单脚趾（其中蹄子就是趾甲）是马成功的进化创新关键。

sentences.en: Rigid, lightweight hooves help with this: they minimize sideways wobble while storing and releasing energy like a spring, much like the shoes a human sprinter might wear, or even the prosthetic running blades sometimes used by amputees.

blocks.html_en: Over millions of years, the number of toes fell gradually from several to just one. Between 43 and 33 million years ago, Mesohippus still sported three toes of roughly equal size, with each touching the ground. By the time of Hipparion, about 23 million years ago, the middle toe carried most of the animal’s weight: the outer two toes had shrunk into vestiges, and the middle toe had become dominant. Finally, Pliohippus took a pivotal step toward the modern form, with a single weight-bearing toe ending in a solid hoof. This evolutionary streamlining produced the feet of today’s horses: a single, sturdy keratin hoof perfectly suited for galloping over open ground.

blocks.html_en: The route to the modern horse involved several detours. Hyracotherium, the progenitor of the horse family, appears in the fossil record in North America from around 55 million years ago, disappearing again 8 million years later. Around 12 million years ago, Hipparion, which, though three-toed, otherwise resembled modern horses, colonized Eurasia. Hippidion, which had short limbs and distinctively shaped facial bones, roamed the plains and mountains of South America from around 3 million years ago. Then, around 2 million years ago, the most recent common ancestor of present-day asses and zebras crossed the Bering land bridge formerly joining Alaska and northeastern Siberia.

blocks.html_en: Although the Americas were home to the earliest proto-horses, horses (including Hippidion and others) later became extinct in the Western Hemisphere around 10,000 years ago, alongside other megafauna like giant sloths, human-sized beavers, and armadillos as big as cars. All horses in the Americas today, including the free-roaming mustangs of the American West, come from European horses introduced after the Spanish conquest – descendants of the branches of the horse family that crossed into Eurasia and avoided extinction.

blocks.html_en: Exactly when, where, and how horses were domesticated remained a mystery until recently, because fossils of wild and early domestic horses look very similar. For decades, archaeologists pointed to the Botai people of northern Kazakhstan, who lived around 5,500 years ago, as the original domesticators. A foal inherits half of its DNA from each of its parents. This is passed on with almost incredible accuracy, with around 2.7 billion base pairs (the data units of DNA) being copied correctly, but even so a few dozen errors creep in each time. Such a pattern signals strong selective pressure: something in the environment consistently favored animals carrying particular versions of genes.

blocks.html_en: One region under heavy selection lies near a gene called ZFPM1, thought to play a role in the development of brain cells involved in mood, fear, and aggression. This suggests that early breeders might have been either deliberately or indirectly choosing animals that were more docile, allowing training, handling, and eventually riding. A second region under strong selection sits just upstream of GSDMC, a gene linked in humans to spinal problems such as chronic back pain and narrowing of the spinal canal. The signal of selection at this locus in horses suggests that breeders may have favored genetic variants associated with stronger, more resilient backs. As horseback riding spread, horses that could bear weight without developing spinal pathologies would have been more desirable.

blocks.html_en: This diversity is the product of millennia of human intervention, selection, and preference, which left distinct traces in the horse’s genome. Compared with many other species, horses have a lot of diversity in the mitochondrial genome, inherited from the mother, but extremely limited variation within the Y chromosome, passed down from father to son. blocks.html_en: In the early Bronze Age, leopard-spotted horses were abundant at Kirklareli-Kanlıgeçit in present-day Turkey. But leopard spotting comes at a cost: horses with two copies of the gene coding for it have night blindness (the inability to see in low light). Its prevalence in certain ancient populations suggests breeders made deliberate choices, where aesthetic or symbolic value outweighed the trait’s practical drawbacks, to favor certain traits unlikely to persist in the wild. Tastes shifted with time: leopard-spotted horses lost their appeal after the early Bronze Age but gained favor in some regions during the Iron Age. And while spotted coats were popular in antiquity, solid chestnut horses prevailed in medieval Western Europe.

sentences.en: And while spotted coats were popular in antiquity, solid chestnut horses prevailed in medieval Western Europe.
sentences.zh: 虽然斑点皮毛在古代很流行，但纯栗色马在中世纪的西欧很流行。

blocks.html_en: In the Middle Ages, horses were inseparable from power and status. Chivalry itself shares an etymological root with the Old French chevalier, literally ‘horseman’. Breeding and maintaining horses became a major industry of nobility and royalty. But they didn’t think in terms of fixed breeds the way we do today. Medieval writers grouped horses by function: the destrier trained for combat, the courser valued for speed, and the palfrey prized for a comfortable ride. Archaeological evidence backs this up. A large study of horse remains from thirteenth- and fourteenth-century London shows a range of sizes and builds, not the uniformity that we would expect from tightly restricted breeding.

blocks.html_en: Contrary to the modern idea of the medieval warhorse as a massive, towering beast, measurements from excavated horse bones across England show that most stood around 13 to 14.2 hands high, roughly the size of a sturdy modern pony. Even horses associated with elite or military contexts rarely approached the heights of today’s heavy draught breeds. What medieval riders valued instead were animals that were compact (meaning cheap to feed), strong, and agile enough to handle long distances, uneven terrain, and the demands of warfare.

blocks.html_en: By the seventeenth century, horses had been serving human purposes for thousands of years, plowing fields, carrying soldiers, and pulling carts. But in early-modern England, one goal came to dominate: speed. In the 1660s, King Charles II, a fervent horse racing fan, set up a horse breeding and racing center at Newmarket, near London. While horse racing had been popular in previous centuries, Charles II and other racing enthusiasts were the first to methodically breed horses at scale to improve their race performance.

blocks.html_en: Breeders discovered that horses from Arabia, Central Asia, and North Africa were often faster: they were lighter, had a greater drive to run, and were better able to dissipate heat, allowing them to sustain high speeds without overheating. From three exceptional horses imported to England, Byerley Turk (imported in the 1680s), Darley Arabian (1704), and Godolphin Arabian (1729), breeders created the ‘thoroughbred’, a new type of horse designed for speed. Today, 95 percent of all living thoroughbreds are thought to descend from just one of these stallions, Darley Arabian, through his phenomenally successful great-great-grandson, Eclipse.

blocks.html_en: Horse breeding used to be guesswork: breeders paired fast stallions with fast mares and hoped for the best. But in 1791, the General Stud Book started recording every thoroughbred’s ancestry, turning pedigree into data. Breeders could now track bloodlines, deliberately plan matings, and see which combinations actually worked. Thoroughbreds today are defined as horses whose ancestry can be traced entirely to horses listed in the General Stud Book.

blocks.html_en: Harder, better, faster, stronger

sentences.en: Harder, better, faster, stronger
sentences.zh: 更难、更好、更快、更强

blocks.html_en: Racing and breeding evolved side by side. Races in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries involved multiple heats over distances of two to four miles, favoring horses with stamina. Horses didn’t race until they were five or six years old. But by the late eighteenth century, new races like the Derby and the St Leger reset the terms of competition. Horses now raced at three years old, over shorter distances of one to two miles.

sentences.en: Racing and breeding evolved side by side.
sentences.zh: 赛马和育种并行发展。

sentences.zh: 十七世纪和十八世纪的比赛涉及两到四英里的多场预赛，对有耐力的马匹有利。

sentences.zh: 现在马匹在三岁的时候就可以参加一到两英里的短距离比赛。

blocks.html_en: This new format meant an increased premium on speed and precocity, and it has persisted, particularly in the United States and Australia. In Britain and Ireland, the tradition of long-distance races held on in parallel, leading to distinct types: horses that specialize in explosive speed at a young age, classic middle-distance horses, and horses bred for the stamina needed to excel in longer races.

sentences.en: This new format meant an increased premium on speed and precocity, and it has persisted, particularly in the United States and Australia.
sentences.zh: 这种新的形式意味着对速度和早熟的重视程度越来越高，并且它一直持续存在，特别是在美国和澳大利亚。

sentences.en: In Britain and Ireland, the tradition of long-distance races held on in parallel, leading to distinct types: horses that specialize in explosive speed at a young age, classic middle-distance horses, and horses bred for the stamina needed to excel in longer races.
sentences.zh: 在英国和爱尔兰，长距离比赛的传统同时存在，形成了不同的类型：年轻时擅长爆发速度的马、经典的中距离马，以及为在较长距离比赛中脱颖而出所需的耐力而培育的马。

blocks.html_en: After the creation of the thoroughbred and the Stud Book, Anglo-American breeders hit what appears to be an upper limit for speed surprisingly quickly. From the middle of the nineteenth century, when timing and record keeping became good enough to make reliable comparisons, race times improved steadily for about half a century. But although there was consistent improvement, it was small: times only fell by 1 to 2 percent, or 2 to 4 seconds over a 1.5-mile race. Race times for prominent races have not significantly fallen since around 1910. Secretariat’s 1973 Belmont time eclipsed the previous record by a stunning 2.6 seconds. However, the best time since then (Easy Goer in 1989 at 2 minutes 26 seconds) was a full 2 seconds slower than Secretariat’s.

blocks.html_en: Outside the elite, there has been continued improvement: one study found that between 1997 and 2012, accounting for differences such as ground softness and the number of runners, the average British thoroughbred increased its speed by 0.011 yards per second per year. So while we have likely reached the ceiling for how fast an exceptional horse can run, the median horse is beginning to close in on that limit, too.

blocks.html_en: Until 2007, the Stud Book was the cutting edge of horse breeding technology. That changed when scientists sequenced a horse genome for the first time, that of a thoroughbred mare named Twilight. This allowed researchers to study the genetic basis of variation between individual horses far more systematically.

sentences.en: Until 2007, the Stud Book was the cutting edge of horse breeding technology.
sentences.zh: 2007 年之前，种马登记册一直是马匹育种技术的前沿。

sentences.en: That changed when scientists sequenced a horse genome for the first time, that of a thoroughbred mare named Twilight.
sentences.zh: 当科学家首次对马的基因组进行测序时，这种情况发生了变化，这匹马是一匹名叫“暮光”的纯种母马。

sentences.en: This allowed researchers to study the genetic basis of variation between individual horses far more systematically.
sentences.zh: 这使得研究人员能够更系统地研究个体马之间变异的遗传基础。

blocks.html_en: Another step forward in understanding thoroughbred genetics came with a paper published in 2010 that investigated the gene in horses that codes for myostatin, a protein that regulates muscle development. Mice, cattle, dogs, and even humans with mutations in this gene grow outlandishly large muscles because the gene normally acts as a brake on muscle development; with that brake damaged, muscles continue to grow unchecked.

sentences.en: Another step forward in understanding thoroughbred genetics came with a paper published in 2010 that investigated the gene in horses that codes for myostatin, a protein that regulates muscle development.
sentences.zh: 2010 年发表的一篇论文在了解纯种马遗传学方面又向前迈出了一步，该论文研究了马体内编码肌肉生长抑制素（一种调节肌肉发育的蛋白质）的基因。

sentences.en: Mice, cattle, dogs, and even humans with mutations in this gene grow outlandishly large muscles because the gene normally acts as a brake on muscle development; with that brake damaged, muscles continue to grow unchecked.
sentences.zh: 携带该基因突变的小鼠、牛、狗甚至人类都会长出异常巨大的肌肉，因为该基因通常会阻碍肌肉发育。当刹车受损时，肌肉会继续不受控制地生长。

blocks.html_en: The gene coding for myostatin in horses has around 1,100 base pairs. Looking at the exact sequence of this gene, called MSTN, in 148 thoroughbreds revealed that horses could have three different versions of the gene, differing by just one of those base pairs (either a letter ‘C’ or a ‘T’), and that each version was associated with success in different race formats. Horses with two copies of the ‘C’ version tend to be the best sprinters, those with two ‘T’s tend to be high-stamina long-distance runners, and those with one of each tend to fall between the two running profiles.

sentences.en: The gene coding for myostatin in horses has around 1,100 base pairs.
sentences.zh: 马的肌肉生长抑制素基因编码约有 1,100 个碱基对。

sentences.en: Looking at the exact sequence of this gene, called MSTN, in 148 thoroughbreds revealed that horses could have three different versions of the gene, differing by just one of those base pairs (either a letter ‘C’ or a ‘T’), and that each version was associated with success in different race formats.
sentences.zh: 通过观察 148 匹纯种马中这个名为 MSTN 的基因的精确序列，我们发现马可能拥有该基因的三个不同版本，仅因其中一个碱基对（字母“C”或“T”）不同而有所不同，并且每个版本都与不同比赛形式的成功相关。

sentences.en: Horses with two copies of the ‘C’ version tend to be the best sprinters, those with two ‘T’s tend to be high-stamina long-distance runners, and those with one of each tend to fall between the two running profiles.
sentences.zh: 拥有两个“C”版本的马往往是最好的短跑运动员，拥有两个“T”版本的马往往是高耐力的长跑运动员，而拥有两个“T”版本的马往往介于两种跑步模式之间。

blocks.html_en: Later research found that variations in MSTN correspond with different muscle physiology. Horses with the ‘C’ version have a higher proportion of fast-twitch muscle fibers, which enable the explosive bursts of speed required for short-distance sprint racing, while those with the ‘T’ version have a higher proportion of slow-twitch fibers, which allow sustained effort.

sentences.en: Later research found that variations in MSTN correspond with different muscle physiology.
sentences.zh: 后来的研究发现，MSTN 的变化与不同的肌肉生理机能相对应。

sentences.en: Horses with the ‘C’ version have a higher proportion of fast-twitch muscle fibers, which enable the explosive bursts of speed required for short-distance sprint racing, while those with the ‘T’ version have a higher proportion of slow-twitch fibers, which allow sustained effort.
sentences.zh: “C”版本的马具有较高比例的快肌纤维，可以实现短距离冲刺比赛所需的爆发性速度，而“T”版本的马则具有较高比例的慢肌纤维，可以实现持续的努力。

blocks.html_en: Analyzing the DNA of modern horses and museum specimens then showed that the foundation stallions in the Stud Book all had two copies of the ‘T’ variant, and that the ‘C’ mutation probably entered through local British mares. This new variant entered thoroughbred genomes during the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, as English races like the Derby and St Leger got shorter. But the genetic trend is less pronounced in Britain than the United States, where races are rarely longer than 2,000 meters, and especially than in Australia, which favors 1,000 to 1,400-meter lengths. Commercial tests for this gene are now widely used by breeders and trainers.

blocks.html_en: The price of success

sentences.en: The price of success
sentences.zh: 成功的代价

blocks.html_en: Horses’ genetic diversity remained large for thousands of years, before collapsing after the introduction of modern breeding. In nature, diversity is maintained by competing selection pressures that balance one trait against another. A wild horse does not just need to be fast. Its bones need to last. It needs to be resistant to disease. Even a domesticated working horse would, before intensive breeding began, face natural constraints on its traits.

sentences.en: Horses’ genetic diversity remained large for thousands of years, before collapsing after the introduction of modern breeding.
sentences.zh: 马的遗传多样性在数千年来一直保持着巨大的水平，但在引入现代育种后崩溃了。

sentences.en: In nature, diversity is maintained by competing selection pressures that balance one trait against another.
sentences.zh: 在自然界中，多样性是通过平衡一种特征与另一种特征的竞争选择压力来维持的。

sentences.en: A wild horse does not just need to be fast.
sentences.zh: 一匹野马不仅需要跑得快。

sentences.en: Its bones need to last.
sentences.zh: 它的骨头需要持久。

sentences.en: It needs to be resistant to disease.
sentences.zh: 它需要具有抗病能力。

sentences.en: Even a domesticated working horse would, before intensive breeding began, face natural constraints on its traits.
sentences.zh: 即使是驯化的工作马，在集约化繁殖开始之前，其性状也会面临自然限制。

blocks.html_en: In modern thoroughbred breeding, celebrity stallions with the best race records are in high demand. Their owners charge hundreds of thousands of dollars in stud fees, and they can sire perhaps a hundred foals per year. This means that the genes of particular males can quickly sweep to dominance in a population in a way that would be very unusual in nature.

content_html_zh:
1973 年 6 月，栗色小马秘书处在贝尔蒙特锦标赛中跑得如此之快，自此之后没有任何一匹马能与他匹敌。 不到两分半钟，秘书处沿着赛道飞驰，最终拉开距离，以31个长度（近四分之三个足球场）的优势获胜。 其他马匹远远落后，甚至没有出现在电视画面中。 五十年后，数十亿美元已投入育种和培训，但秘书处的记录仍然保持着。

这就是纯种马的悖论：繁育者花了几个世纪的时间试图培育出更快的马，但在这样做的过程中，他们可能已经培育出了让马不断进步甚至保持健壮的遗传多样性。

正在进行的工作通讯

将来自“正在进行的工作”的新文章发送到您的收件箱。

这个悖论并不局限于赛道。 马最初是一种梗类大小、多趾的森林居民，经过超过 5500 万年的进化和几千年的人类干预，变成了从紧凑的冰岛小马到流线型赛马的各种形式。 在这段历史的大部分时间里，自然选择慢慢地塑造了马。 直到最近，人类的野心才开始显现，培育出速度、耐力和温顺的动物。 其结果是在形式和性能上产生了非凡的多样性，但遗传多样性也急剧缩小。

第一批马

故事开始于 5500 万年前，位于现在北美洲覆盖的温暖潮湿的森林深处。 你很难认出最早的马。 它被称为 Hyracotherium，身高只有 14 英寸，更接近梗犬而不是现代马。 它的前脚有四个脚趾，后脚有三个脚趾，非常适合在柔软的沼泽地面上小心翼翼地移动并啃咬水果和树叶。

18 至 1500 万年前，当全球气温上升时，马科动物多样化为 20 多个属（生活在林地和稀树草原的物种之上的细分）。 这些谱系中的大多数早已灭绝：今天，只有马属幸存下来，其中包括马、斑马、驴和驴。

随着草原的扩张，经过数百万年，马科动物进化成了我们今天看到的马。 很少有进化故事有如此详细的记录。 十九世纪，当古生物学家 OC 马什在美国西部发掘出丰富的马化石时，它们的重要性立即得到了认识。 这里几乎一步一步地展现了进化的过程：马从小型多趾森林居民转变为大型单趾动物，它们吃草而不是吃水果和树叶。

单脚趾（其中蹄子就是趾甲）是马成功的进化创新关键。 平原上的生活有利于能够高效长距离奔跑的动物。 刚性、轻质的蹄子有助于做到这一点：它们可以像弹簧一样储存和释放能量，同时最大限度地减少侧向摆动，就像人类短跑运动员可能穿的鞋子，甚至截肢者有时使用的假肢跑步刀片。

数百万年来，脚趾的数量逐渐从几个减少到只有一个。 43 至 3300 万年前，中马仍然拥有三个大小大致相等的脚趾，每个脚趾都接触地面。 到了大约 2300 万年前的三趾马时代，中趾承担了动物的大部分重量：外侧的两个脚趾已经萎缩成遗迹，而中趾则占据了主导地位。 最后，Pliohippus 向现代形态迈出了关键的一步，其单个承重脚趾的末端是坚固的蹄子。 这种进化的流线型产生了今天的马的脚：一个坚固的角蛋白蹄，非常适合在开阔的地面上驰骋。

通往现代马的道路绕了好几条弯路。 始祖马是马科的祖先，大约 5500 万年前就出现在北美的化石记录中，800 万年后再次消失。 大约 1200 万年前，三趾马在欧亚大陆殖民，虽然它长着三趾，但在其他方面与现代马很相似。 希皮迪翁（Hippidion）四肢短小，面部骨骼形状独特，大约从 300 万年前开始就在南美洲的平原和山脉中漫步。 然后，大约 200 万年前，当今驴和斑马的最新共同祖先跨越了以前连接阿拉斯加和西伯利亚东北部的白令陆桥。

在接下来的五十万年里，他们的后代迅速扩展到欧亚大陆，并至少两次进入非洲。 第一次迁徙的后代多样化为各种斑马，而第二次迁徙则产生了现代驴和非洲野驴。

尽管美洲是最早的原始马的家园，但马（包括希皮迪翁和其他马）后来在大约一万年前在西半球灭绝，与其他巨型动物一起灭绝的还有巨型树懒、人类大小的海狸和汽车那么大的犰狳。 今天美洲的所有马，包括美国西部自由漫游的野马，都来自于西班牙征服后引入的欧洲马——是跨入欧亚大陆并避免灭绝的马科分支的后代。

第一个驯马师

直到最近，马的确切驯化时间、地点和方式仍然是个谜，因为野马和早期驯马的化石看起来非常相似。 几十年来，考古学家指出生活在大约 5500 年前的哈萨克斯坦北部的博泰人是最早的驯化者。 挖掘工作中发现了畜栏、可能存在马具的证据，甚至还发现了残留有马奶的陶器，这清楚地表明波泰人不仅狩猎和食用野马，而且已将野马融入了他们生活的许多方面。

虽然波泰马看起来像是现代马的明显祖先，但 DNA 讲述了一个不同的故事：当科学家对波泰遗址的 20 匹马的基因组进行测序时，它们在基因上与现代家养品种并不相似。 相反，博泰马与普氏野马（发音为 shuh-VAHL-ski）密切相关，普氏野马是 1870 年代末在蒙古草原上发现的一种马，长期以来被认为是唯一真正的野马。

这意味着，与人们长期以来认为普氏野马是最后幸存的真正野马的观点相反，它们实际上是在博泰发现的最早已知家马的野生亲戚。 虽然波泰人很可能首先驯化了马，但他们的文化消失了，他们的马又回到了野外。

从草原到马厩

我们所认识和喜爱的马来自不同的来源。 一千多年后，即大约 4,200 年前，他们出现在现在俄罗斯南部的东欧大草原上，这个地区诞生了哥萨克、金帐汗国和匈奴等著名的骑马战士。

科学家们通过对古马遗骸的基因分析，结合碳测年法确定了它们的精确年龄，从而弄清楚了这一点。 小马驹从父母那里继承了一半的 DNA。 这种传递的精确度几乎令人难以置信，大约 27 亿个碱基对（DNA 的数据单元）被正确复制，但即便如此，每次还是会出现几十个错误。 科学家可以从化石中取出远古祖先的 DNA，将其与现代后代的 DNA 进行比较，然后通过计算累积的突变数量来估计已经过去了多少代。

2021 年，科学家们做到了这一点，对 273 组骨头的基因组进行了测序，这些骨头的年龄从 50,000 年到 200 年不等。 通过观察骨骼的突变率和碳测年来确认它们的确切年龄，他们可以计算出世代流逝的速度。 大约 4,200 年前，世代时钟开始比野马快两倍，相对于野马减半，这表明有人有意繁殖。

尽管骨骼无法告诉我们古代马的行为方式，但它们的基因组为我们提供了线索。 研究人员发现，某些基因变异在这些草原马身上变得异常普遍。 这种模式标志着强烈的选择压力：环境中的某些东西始终偏爱携带特定版本基因的动物。

一个受到严格选择的区域位于一种名为 ZFPM1 的基因附近，该基因被认为在涉及情绪、恐惧和攻击性的脑细胞发育中发挥着重要作用。 这表明早期饲养者可能有意或间接地选择了更温顺的动物，以便进行训练、操作和最终骑乘。 第二个受到强烈选择的区域位于 GSDMC 的上游，GSDMC 是人类与慢性背痛和椎管狭窄等脊柱问题相关的基因。 马的这个基因座的选择信号表明，饲养者可能偏爱与更强壮、更有弹性的背部相关的遗传变异。 随着骑马的普及，能够承受重量而不患脊柱疾病的马会更受欢迎。

这些草原马被遗传学家称为 DOM2（即驯化谱系二），像野火一样蔓延开来。 到公元前 2200 年至 2000 年，DOM2 基因谱从其起源地区传播到安纳托利亚、多瑙河下游地区和波西米亚。

考古证据表明，随着 DOM2 的扩张，其他野马的数量逐渐减少。 到公元前 1500-1000 年左右，几乎所有这些都被吸收或取代。 分布于东欧的塔潘马于 1909 年灭绝。 到了 1969 年，普氏野马被宣布在野外灭绝。 所有现存的普氏原羚马均源自 1900 年左右捕获的 15 匹马。 直到1992年，大约2000只的后代才开始被重新引入欧亚大草原。

世界各地发现的许多所谓的野马种群，包括野马、紫貂岛小马和澳大利亚野马，都是现代家养马的后代，这些马在过去几个世纪中再次变得野性。

课程用马

随着时间的推移，人类培育出了具有多种表型的独特马品种，从肩部高度仅一米的阿根廷小马，到能够拖拉数吨的法国佩尔什马；从具有标准步态（步行、小跑、慢跑和疾驰）的马到能够执行替代步态的马，例如漫步，没有弹跳，使它们骑起来更舒适。 冰岛马的语气非常平稳，骑手可以拎起整杯啤酒而不会洒出一滴。

这种多样性是人类数千年干预、选择和偏好的产物，在马的基因组中留下了独特的痕迹。 与许多其他物种相比，马的线粒体基因组具有很多多样性，从母亲遗传而来，但Y染色体内的变异极其有限，从父亲遗传给儿子。 这种对比表明了一种驯化模式：许多当地母马（母马）与相当有限的种马（雄性）繁殖，集中父系血统，同时保留母系血统的多样性。

古代 DNA 为我们提供了一个超越化石的窗口，使我们能够追踪表型如何以化石记录中未显示的方式发生变化。 除了人类之外，马是古代基因组学研究最多的物种之一。 事实上，首次成功地回收和分析古代 DNA 是在 1984 年，从已灭绝的斑驴（斑马的近亲）的 150 年前的组织中进行的——比古代人类 DNA 实现同样的目标还要早一年。 成功恢复和解码的最古老的基因组之一来自于育空地区永久冻土层中保存超过 50 万年的马骨。

毛色为了解早期马匹繁殖提供了另一个窗口。 在现存的马中，颜色和图案背后的基因，如豹纹、托比亚诺斑块（如牛的颜色）和奶油色稀释液（使马皮毛的颜色变浅），都是众所周知的。 早在驯化开始之前，旧石器时代晚期的野马就出现了暗褐色（灰金色或棕褐色）、黑色和豹纹斑点的基因变异。

在青铜时代早期，在今天的土耳其的 Kirklareli-Kanlıgeçit 地区，豹斑马数量众多。 但发现豹子是有代价的：拥有两份豹子编码基因的马患有夜盲症（在弱光下无法看见）。 它在某些古代种群中的流行表明，育种者做出了深思熟虑的选择，其中美学或象征价值超过了该性状的实际缺点，以偏爱某些不太可能在野外持续存在的性状。 人们的口味随着时间的推移而发生变化：在青铜时代早期之后，豹纹马就失去了吸引力，但在铁器时代却在一些地区受到青睐。 虽然斑点皮毛在古代很流行，但纯栗色马在中世纪的西欧很流行。

在中世纪，马与权力和地位密不可分。 骑士精神本身与古法语chevalier（字面意思是“骑士”）有着共同的词源。 饲养和饲养马匹成为贵族和皇室的主要产业。 但他们并没有像我们今天那样考虑固定品种。 中世纪的作家根据马的功能对马进行分类：战马以战斗为目的，骏马以速度为价值，而马则以舒适的骑行为价值。 考古证据支持了这一点。 对十三世纪和十四世纪伦敦的马遗骸进行的一项大型研究表明，马匹的大小和体型各不相同，而不是我们所期望的严格限制繁殖的一致性。

现代人认为中世纪战马是一种巨大而高耸的野兽，但对英格兰各地出土的马骨进行的测量显示，大多数战马高约 13 至 14.2 英尺，大约相当于一匹强壮的现代小马的大小。 即使是与精英或军事背景相关的马也很少能达到当今重役品种的高度。 相反，中世纪的骑手看重的是紧凑（意味着饲养成本低廉）、强壮且敏捷的动物，足以应对长距离、不平坦的地形和战争的要求。

对速度的需求

到了十七世纪，马已经为人类服务了数千年，耕田、运载士兵、拉车。 但在近代早期的英格兰，一个目标占据了主导地位：速度。 1660 年代，狂热的赛马爱好者国王查理二世在伦敦附近的纽马基特建立了马匹繁育和赛马中心。 虽然赛马在前几个世纪就很流行，但查理二世和其他赛马爱好者是第一个有条不紊地大规模饲养马匹以提高其比赛成绩的人。

饲养员发现，来自阿拉伯、中亚和北非的马通常速度更快：它们更轻，奔跑动力更强，散热能力更好，使它们能够维持高速而不会过热。 饲养员从进口到英国的三匹特殊马匹——拜尔利土耳其马（Byerley Turk，1680 年代进口）、达利阿拉伯马（Darley Rabian，1704 年）和戈多芬阿拉伯马（Godolphin Rabian，1729 年）中培育出“纯种马”，这是一种专为速度而设计的新型马。 如今，95% 的现存纯种马都被认为是其中一匹种马达利·阿拉伯 (Darley Rabian) 及其非凡成功的曾曾孙 Eclipse 的后代。

过去，马的育种是靠猜测：饲养员将跑得快的公马与跑得快的母马配对，并希望得到最好的结果。 但从 1791 年开始，通用种马登记册开始记录每匹纯种马的血统，将血统变成数据。 育种者现在可以追踪血统，有意识地计划交配，并看看哪些组合实际上有效。 今天的纯种马被定义为血统完全可以追溯到通用种马名录中列出的马的马。

更难、更好、更快、更强

赛马和育种并行发展。 十七世纪和十八世纪的比赛涉及两到四英里的多场预赛，对有耐力的马匹有利。 马要到五六岁才参加比赛。 但到了十八世纪末，像德比和圣莱杰这样的新比赛重新设定了比赛条件。 现在马匹在三岁的时候就可以参加一到两英里的短距离比赛。

这种新的形式意味着对速度和早熟的重视程度越来越高，并且它一直持续存在，特别是在美国和澳大利亚。 在英国和爱尔兰，长距离比赛的传统同时存在，形成了不同的类型：年轻时擅长爆发速度的马、经典的中距离马，以及为在较长距离比赛中脱颖而出所需的耐力而培育的马。

在创建纯种马和种马名册后，英美育种者以惊人的速度达到了速度的上限。 从十九世纪中叶开始，计时和记录保存变得足够好，可以进行可靠的比较，比赛时间在大约半个世纪的时间里稳步提高。 尽管持续改善，但进步很小：时间仅下降了 1% 到 2%，即在 1.5 英里的比赛中下降了 2 到 4 秒。 自 1910 年左右以来，重要赛事的比赛时间并没有显着下降。 秘书处 1973 年贝尔蒙特时间以 2.6 秒的惊人成绩超越了之前的记录。 然而，此后的最佳成绩（1989 年 Easy Goer 成绩为 2 分 26 秒）比秘书处慢了整整 2 秒。

除了精英之外，也有持续的进步：一项研究发现，1997 年至 2012 年间，考虑到地面松软度和跑步者数量等差异，英国纯种马的速度平均每年提高 0.011 码。 因此，虽然我们可能已经达到了优秀马匹跑速的上限，但中等马匹也开始接近这个极限。

速度基因

2007 年之前，种马登记册一直是马匹育种技术的前沿。 当科学家首次对马的基因组进行测序时，这种情况发生了变化，这匹马是一匹名叫“暮光”的纯种母马。 这使得研究人员能够更系统地研究个体马之间变异的遗传基础。

2010 年发表的一篇论文在了解纯种马遗传学方面又向前迈出了一步，该论文研究了马体内编码肌肉生长抑制素（一种调节肌肉发育的蛋白质）的基因。 携带该基因突变的小鼠、牛、狗甚至人类都会长出异常巨大的肌肉，因为该基因通常会阻碍肌肉发育。当刹车受损时，肌肉会继续不受控制地生长。

马的肌肉生长抑制素基因编码约有 1,100 个碱基对。 通过观察 148 匹纯种马中这个名为 MSTN 的基因的精确序列，我们发现马可能拥有该基因的三个不同版本，仅因其中一个碱基对（字母“C”或“T”）不同而有所不同，并且每个版本都与不同比赛形式的成功相关。 拥有两个“C”版本的马往往是最好的短跑运动员，拥有两个“T”版本的马往往是高耐力的长跑运动员，而拥有两个“T”版本的马往往介于两种跑步模式之间。

后来的研究发现，MSTN 的变化与不同的肌肉生理机能相对应。 “C”版本的马具有较高比例的快肌纤维，可以实现短距离冲刺比赛所需的爆发性速度，而“T”版本的马则具有较高比例的慢肌纤维，可以实现持续的努力。

对现代马匹和博物馆标本的 DNA 分析表明，种马簿中的基础种马都有两个“T”变体副本，而“C”突变可能是通过当地的英国母马进入的。 这种新的变体在十八世纪末和十九世纪进入纯种马基因组，因为像德比和圣莱杰这样的英国赛马变得越来越矮。 但这种遗传趋势在英国不如美国那么明显，美国的比赛长度很少超过 2,000 米，尤其是与澳大利亚相比，澳大利亚更喜欢 1,000 至 1,400 米的长度。 该基因的商业测试现在被饲养员和训练员广泛使用。

成功的代价

马的遗传多样性在数千年来一直保持着巨大的水平，但在引入现代育种后崩溃了。 在自然界中，多样性是通过平衡一种特征与另一种特征的竞争选择压力来维持的。 一匹野马不仅需要跑得快。 它的骨头需要持久。 它需要具有抗病能力。 即使是驯化的工作马，在集约化繁殖开始之前，其性状也会面临自然限制。

在现代纯种马育种中，拥有最佳比赛记录的名人种马的需求量很大。 他们的主人收取数十万美元的种马费用，他们每年大约可以繁育一百匹小马驹。 这意味着特定雄性的基因可以迅速以一种在自然界中非常不寻常的方式在种群中占据主导地位。

随着多样性的丧失，现代马由于在小群体中繁殖而积累了有害的突变。 马和人类一样，反复的近亲繁殖集中了有害特征，因为彼此有血缘关系的父母更有可能共享相同的突变，导致后代拥有两个突变基因拷贝，而不是一个突变拷贝和一个正常拷贝，这可能掩盖突变的影响。

对所有澳大利亚纯种马（超过 135,000 匹马）的基因分析表明，近亲繁殖与速度较慢、时间较短和利润较低的职业生涯相关。 令人惊奇的是，澳大利亚纯种马的近亲繁殖中 80% 以上是由 10 个 18 世纪的祖先进行的。 育种者并非对这些风险视而不见。 例如，美国夸特马协会要求对种马进行多种遗传疾病检测。

由于遗传学在马匹育种中发挥了如此重要的作用，因此马匹育种者不断追随科学前沿也就不足为奇了。 世界上第一匹克隆马 Prometea 于 2003 年诞生。 尽管美国赛马俱乐部禁止，但克隆马现在已成为一项大生意，因为其他马术运动，包括障碍赛和马球，都允许克隆。

2024 年，阿根廷公司 Kheiron 宣布生产出第一批 CRISPR 编辑的马：Polo Pureza，一匹屡获殊荣的母马，它是五种速度更快的基因编辑克隆的基础。 据报道，该公司修改了 MSTN 基因，使动物能够发育出更多的肌肉纤维，从而可能跑得更快。 即便如此，通过基因编辑打破当前记录的前景仍然渺茫。 今天的赛马已经针对速度进行了严格优化，平衡了力量与携带额外肌肉质量的成本。 增加更多肌肉是相对容易实现的目标，如果这是解锁更快速度的关键，选择性育种可能已经实现了这一目标。

纯种悖论

在 1973 年的贝尔蒙特锦标赛上，秘书处以自己的方式参赛。 他的非凡表现似乎是许多看似不可能的因素共同作用的结果。 据报道，Secretariat 去世后，他的心脏重达近 10 公斤，是正常情况的两倍。 然而，这似乎是一种生理上的侥幸，因为它不是可靠地遗传给后代的特征。 加上他非凡的耐力、异常强大的双腿（使他每步可跑 25 英尺）、有利的比赛条件以及熟练的骑师，尽管在育种、训练、营养和兽医护理方面取得了进步，但半个世纪后，他的比赛时间仍然无人能敌。

秘书处让我们一睹生物学的上限。 但随着赛马突破这一极限，变得更快、更强大，它们的种群也随着基因库的缩小而变得更加脆弱。 我们四千年来对终极马的追求可能已经没有多久了。
